opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that analogy is actually quite apt, and it gets at something important about how intelligence works. If you look at structure mapping, the Gentner-style view of analogy, what you're doing is taking a relational structure from one domain and aligning it with another. The solar system and the atom: you keep the relations, something orbits something more massive, and you swap out the objects. That's very much like having a template with slots and filling them in with whatever fits the current situation.

Case-based reasoning is similar. You have a library of past cases, you retrieve the one most similar to your current problem, and then you adapt it. The adaptation step is essentially ad-libbing: you keep the skeleton of the old solution and improvise the parts that don't match.

What I find interesting is that this is also, to a large extent, what large language models are doing. People argue about whether they're "just" memorizing or genuinely reasoning, but I think the truth is in between. They've absorbed an enormous number of structures, patterns of argument, story templates, code idioms, and when you give them a prompt they find something that fits and fill in the blanks. That's why they're so fluent, and also why they fail in characteristic ways: when the problem requires a structure they haven't seen, or the mapping is subtle, they pattern-match to the wrong template and confidently produce something that looks right but isn't.

So in my view, analogy is one of the five tribes of machine learning for a reason, and it's arguably the most underrated one. But it isn't the whole story. Filling in blanks in a structure is powerful, but you also need the ability to compose structures, to build new ones from logical primitives, to reason about uncertainty when the mapping is ambiguous. The ad-libbing works best when you have a rich enough repertoire of structures, and the deep question is where those structures come from in the first place. That's where you need something more like symbolic induction or learning in a genuinely compositional way. The master algorithm, if we get there, will have to unify all of that: the analogical matching, the logic, the probabilistic reasoning, the gradient-based learning. Each of them alone is ad-libbing with a limited script.

r001.rationale: The response describes aligning relational structure from one domain with another, preserving the relations while substituting the objects, and also describes adapting a retrieved case. This communicates combining substantial pieces through structure mapping or case-based reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the analogy is actually quite apt, but it also reveals exactly where the two paradigms part ways. Case-based reasoning, in its purest form, says: here's a new situation, find the most similar past situation, and adapt its solution. Structure mapping, Dedre Gentner's work, is the more sophisticated version of that, where similarity isn't about surface features but about the relational structure. You're mapping the solar system onto the atom, not because they look alike, but because the relations line up: something big in the center, smaller things orbiting around it due to an attractive force.

Now, the ad-libbing picture, filling in blanks in a general structure, is really the symbolic view of the same thing, approached from the opposite direction. The symbolist says: I have a schema, a template, a logical rule with variables, and I instantiate it. The analogizer says: I don't have the template in advance, I have the examples, and the template emerges when I line two of them up and see what's shared. So in a sense they meet in the middle. An analogy is a schema you haven't bothered to abstract yet, and a schema is an analogy you've abstracted so thoroughly you've forgotten the examples it came from.

Where I think the ad-libbing metaphor is a little misleading is that it makes it sound like the hard part is the filling-in, and the structure is given. In real reasoning, the hard part is figuring out which structure applies in the first place. That's the retrieval and mapping problem, and it's where case-based reasoning spends most of its effort. A jazz musician ad-libbing isn't just filling slots in a fixed chord progression, they're deciding, on the fly, which of a thousand fragments they've internalized is the right one to bend to this moment. That's analogy, not template completion.

And frankly, I think this is what large language models are doing, whether their builders want to describe it that way or not. They've absorbed an enormous library of cases, and what comes out is a kind of structure mapping over them: the new prompt is aligned with patterns in the training distribution, and the gaps are filled in. The difference from classical case-based reasoning is that the cases and the templates are all smeared together in the weights rather than stored discretely. Which is a strength, because the similarity measure is learned instead of handcrafted, and a weakness, because you lose the ability to say: here's the specific case I'm reasoning from, and here's why the mapping is valid.

So my view is that the analogy is right, and the goal of unifying the paradigms is precisely to have both: the fluid, learned similarity of the connectionists, and the explicit, inspectable structure of the symbolists. Neither one alone is the master algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response describes comparing examples, mapping relational structure, and adapting a past solution. It does not clearly say that the method can operate by combining two substantial pieces.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a useful analogy there, but filling in the blanks is really the easy part. If somebody gives you a structure and tells you which slots to fill, a lot of the work has already been done. In case-based reasoning, you have to find a relevant previous case, decide which parts correspond to the new situation, and then adapt it. And in structure mapping, the interesting thing is often that the correspondence is between relationships, rather than between objects that look alike.

So you could say that analogy is a kind of ad-libbing, but you’re also figuring out which script to use and how to change it. That’s where a lot of the intelligence comes in. A good analogy lets you carry something over from the old situation that you hadn’t already recognized in the new one. It gives you an inference, not just a way of redescribing what you already know.

r001.rationale: The response describes finding a relevant prior case, mapping relationships, and adapting it, but does not identify combining two substantial pieces as a way the process operates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a useful analogy. In case-based reasoning, you take a situation you’ve encountered before and adapt it to the situation you’re facing now. So, in that sense, you’re filling in the blanks. But the interesting question is: how do you decide what the blanks are, and what should go into them?

With structure mapping, the correspondence is between relationships, not just individual objects. You might have two situations that look very different on the surface but share a relational structure. Recognizing that structure lets you transfer something you know about one situation to the other.

So ad-libbing within a template captures part of it. But a lot of the intelligence is in finding the right template, deciding which parts to preserve, and figuring out where the analogy breaks down. Once somebody has handed you the structure and marked all the blanks, they’ve already done a substantial part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes adapting a prior situation and transferring knowledge through relational structure, but it does not identify combining two substantial pieces as a way this can operate.
